\section{Introduction}
Benchmark suites~\cite{PTS,smith2011byte,kopytov2004sysbench} characterize modern computing platforms by running standardized workloads across processors, memory, storage, system software, and accelerators to produce a repeatable performance profile beyond any single measurement. Such suites are widely used in performance-critical infrastructure workflows, including cloud instance comparison~\cite{aslanpour2020performance,lenk2011you,hwang2015cloud,marieska2011performance,papadopoulos2019methodological,moschetta2012ofbench,alhamazani2015cross}, monitoring~\cite{baruwal2016smart,}, and performance autotuning~\cite{wang2023keentune,openeuler_atune_readme_zh,chen2024autoos,sun2025kconfigtune}. However, the same breadth that makes benchmark suites useful also makes them costly to execute in full. Comprehensive suites often contain many heterogeneous workloads, each consuming wall-clock time and contending for CPU cores, memory bandwidth, storage bandwidth, or accelerator resources. While this cost may be acceptable for occasional offline evaluation, it becomes difficult to amortize when benchmarking must be repeated across many machines, instance types, software revisions, configurations, or time intervals. In deployed or shared environments, full-suite execution can also perturb the system being measured by competing for resources, interfering with co-located workloads, or changing thermal and frequency states. Moreover, conventional suites largely follow an all-or-nothing execution model: they run a fixed set of workloads and produce meaningful results only after the full run completes.





We present \ourmethod, a benchmarking methodology and toolchain that reframes full-suite execution as a selective-measurement and reconstruction problem.
Given a snapshot of the target machine state, combining conventional system information with low-overhead runtime signals gathered through eBPF. Conditioned on this
snapshot, a router selects a small subset of suite components to execute. A reconstruction model then uses the resulting partial observations to predict the missing component results and recover the aggregate suite-level score. This design reduces cost in two complementary ways: horizontally, by executing only a compact set of informative workloads; and vertically, by replacing unexecuted measurements with model-based prediction. The approach is inspired by the sparse activation principle of mixture-of-experts models, but applies that intuition to reproducible commodity benchmark pipelines rather than neural forward passes.




\section{Background and Motivation}

\subsection{Benchmark Suites}

Benchmark suites provide reproducible and quantifiable measurements for comparing system performance across machines, configurations, and software versions. Rather than relying on a single workload, a suite decomposes system performance into multiple components, each targeting a specific workload pattern or subsystem, such as computation, memory, storage, networking, process control, or inter-process communication. We denote a suite as
\[
\mathcal{B}=\{b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_N\},
\]
where \(b_i\) is the \(i\)-th component.

For a system state \(s\), the full result of component \(b_i\) is
\[
y_i = f_i(s,T_i,\epsilon_i),
\]
where \(T_i\) is the execution budget required by the original benchmark protocol and \(\epsilon_i\) denotes measurement noise. A full-suite run produces
\[
\mathbf{y}=[y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_N],
\]
and, when defined by the benchmark framework, an aggregate score
\[
Y=A(\mathbf{y}).
\]

The cost of full-suite benchmarking comes from two sources: the number of components and the duration of each component. Formally,
\[
C_{\mathrm{full}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}C_i(T_i).
\]
This cost can be substantial for suites with many components or long measurement intervals. However, not all observations are equally informative. Components may stress overlapping subsystems and therefore exhibit correlated results, while short executions may already expose the rate or latency trend of a full run. This motivates our design goal: estimate the full component vector and aggregate score using only sparse component observations and short execution windows.


\subsection{Motivation}
\paragraph{Observation 1: Full execution is expensive.}
In Unix-like operating systems, we use UnixBench as a representative full-suite system benchmark. Originating from the BYTE UNIX benchmark suite, UnixBench remains a widely used open-source benchmark for evaluating system-level performance. It has been adopted in practical system tuning projects such as A-Tune~\cite{openeuler_atune_readme_zh} and KeenTune~\cite{wang2023keentune}. Figure~\ref{fig:tuning_breakdown_pies} reports the time breakdown of a typical KeenTune auto-tuning task. The results show that UnixBench evaluation dominates the overall tuning process, while the model tuning time accounts for only a small fraction. Since auto-tuning usually invokes the benchmark repeatedly to compare different configurations, the accumulated evaluation overhead quickly becomes unacceptable(Table~\ref{tab:fullsuite_execution_time}). Also, running the full suite consumes substantial system resources and can interfere with co-located applications. This makes full execution unsuitable for production-time detection.

\paragraph{Observation 2: Full-suite scores are often unnecessary.}
A full-suite benchmark usually aggregates the results of many heterogeneous components into a single overall score. However, for a specific workload or tuning objective, this aggregate score may not be the most meaningful optimization target. For example, a web service is usually more sensitive to request handling, process scheduling, networking, and memory behavior, while a compilation workload is more sensitive to process creation, filesystem activity, and CPU throughput. Optimizing the overall score may therefore waste measurements on components that have little relevance to the target workload, or even obscure the performance changes of the components that matter.

\paragraph{Observation 3: Metrics converge before full completion.}
Even when benchmark evaluation is needed, executing a selected component to completion is not always necessary. Many components are iterative rate tests rather than one-shot tasks. For example, Dhrystone and Whetstone in UnixBench~\cite{smith2011byte} repeatedly execute integer and floating-point operation kernels and report an operation rate. In these components, the final metric is computed from accumulated work over an execution interval. Therefore, a short prefix already contains direct information about the same rate that will be reported at the end of the full run. If the prefix rate becomes stable, continuing the benchmark mainly reduces statistical uncertainty rather than changing the measured quantity itself. This suggests that benchmark execution can be reduced vertically by estimating full-run metrics from short-run observations.

\label{sec:methods}

\subsection{Overview}
\label{subsec:method-overview}

\ourmethod approximates a complete benchmark run by observing only a small subset of informative sub-benchmarks. 
Given a target system, it first collects a system feature vector \(x\), which captures static platform properties and lightweight runtime state. 
A router then ranks the benchmark subtests and selects a small subset for observation (Section~\ref{subsec:router}). 
The selected subtests are executed normally or evaluated through a fixed-duration probe (Section~\ref{subsec:time-bounded-probing}). 
The observed results are encoded as sparse score-time pairs and passed to a reconstructor, which predicts all subtest scores and the aggregate suite score (Section~\ref{subsec:reconstructor}).

\ourmethod separates offline training from online evaluation. 
During offline training, complete benchmark runs provide supervision for all model components. 
The router learns to identify informative subtests, the probe estimator learns to predict full subtest scores from short-window telemetry, and the reconstructor learns to recover full-suite results from partial observations. 
During online evaluation, the trained models are reused on a new target system, so \ourmethod only needs to profile the system and observe the selected subtests instead of running the entire benchmark suite.

\subsection{Feature Collection and Engineering}

Feature collection provides the contextual information required to reduce benchmark cost while preserving the ability to estimate full-suite performance. The framework observes three factors that affect measured performance: what the machine is, what state the machine is in, and how a benchmark behaves during its initial execution prefix.

For the $i$-th benchmark run, we define the system context vector as
$$
\mathbf{x}_i = [\mathbf{x}_i^{\mathrm{static}}, \mathbf{x}_i^{\mathrm{dynamic}}]
$$
where $\mathbf{x}_i^{\mathrm{static}}$ describes stable host properties (e.g., CPU topology, total memory, OS versions) and $\mathbf{x}_i^{\mathrm{dynamic}}$ captures the transient runtime state before benchmark execution (e.g., system load, hardware counters). The vector $\mathbf{x}_i$ is collected once before a full-suite run and is used by both the benchmark router and the early-stopping estimator.

During short-run probing, the framework further collects a probe-specific vector $\mathbf{p}_{i,j}$ for benchmark component $b_j$. Unlike $\mathbf{x}_i$, which describes the global context of the $i$-th run, $\mathbf{p}_{i,j}$ summarizes the execution prefix of a specific component, capturing wall-clock time, context-switch rates, and categorical identifiers. Table~\ref{tab:feature_collection} summarizes these feature groups by collection stage and purpose.

\paragraph{Feature Processing and Domain-Aware Scaling.}
Raw system telemetry cannot be directly fed into the models. Instead of applying global statistical normalization (e.g., MinMax or standard scaling) which obscures physical limits across heterogeneous machines, \ourmethod employs domain-aware semantic scaling. Static hardware capacities (e.g., total CPU cores, memory sizes converted to uniform units) preserve their original magnitudes to explicitly inform the model of the system's ceiling. Dynamic metrics are transformed into stable ratios or rates: transient CPU utilization and I/O wait times are mapped to percentage ratios, while monotonically increasing counters (e.g., page faults, context switches, PMU instructions) are converted to per-second rates. Categorical variables, such as workload types or probe flags, are handled via one-hot encoding. All missing values are zero-filled to maintain a deterministic tensor shape for inference.

\paragraph{Cost-Aware Collection and Fallbacks.}
Extracting high-fidelity telemetry, such as PMU (Performance Monitoring Unit) events or eBPF traces, incurs overhead and relies on specific kernel configurations. Rather than statistically pruning these informative features, \ourmethod adopts an engineering-driven fallback strategy to balance extraction cost and prediction accuracy. If high-overhead \texttt{perf} counters are unavailable or blocked by the hypervisor, the collector safely degrades to standard \texttt{/proc} statistics. Similarly, if eBPF tracing is disabled or GPU telemetry is absent on CPU-only instances, the framework zero-masks the corresponding vector dimensions. This robust collection pipeline ensures that the benchmarking methodology remains lightweight and executable across strictly isolated cloud tenants or bare-metal machines without crashing the evaluation process.


\subsection{Router: Conditional Expert Selection}
\label{subsec:router}

A full benchmark suite contains inherent redundancy. Although each sub-benchmark targets a specific subsystem, their results are jointly determined by the underlying system state---such as CPU throughput, memory hierarchy, and scheduler behavior. For example, in UnixBench, \texttt{dhry2reg} and \texttt{whetstone-double} reflect computation, while \texttt{pipe} and \texttt{syscall} reflect OS-level overheads. Because these sub-benchmarks are different projections of the same system configuration, a carefully selected subset preserves sufficient information to estimate the behavior of the full suite.

However, the most informative subset is not statically fixed. A CPU-bound configuration may require different representative tests than an I/O-bound configuration. \ourmethod formulates benchmark acceleration as a conditional selection problem: given the current system feature vector $x$, dynamically select a small subset of sub-benchmarks that provides the highest utility for reconstructing the full-suite result.

\paragraph{Mixture-of-Experts Formulation and Learning-to-Rank.}
We adopt a mixture-of-experts view, treating each independently executable sub-benchmark as a measurement expert within a fixed pool:
$$
\mathcal{E}=\{e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_n\}
$$
Each expert is represented as $e_i=(\texttt{test\_id}_i, r_i, c_i)$, where $r_i$ is the observed score and $c_i$ is its execution cost.

Crucially, \ourmethod does not treat routing as a standard multi-class classification problem. The goal is not to assign a single ``best'' label to a system state, but to evaluate the conditional relevance of \textit{all} available tests and select the Top-$K$ subset. Given $x$, the router assigns a relevance score to each expert, $s_i=f_{\theta}(x, e_i)$, and converts these into selection probabilities:
$$
p_i=\frac{\exp(s_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\exp(s_j)}
$$
\ourmethod then isolates the Top-$K$ experts to execute:
$$
\mathcal{S}_K(x)=\operatorname{TopK}_{e_i \in \mathcal{E}} p_i
$$

\paragraph{Model Exploration and Lightweight Architecture.}
To capture the non-linear interactions between system features and benchmark behavior, \ourmethod explores three lightweight routing architectures, intentionally bypassing heavy Large Language Models (LLMs) or exhaustive AutoML searches to ensure inference latency remains negligible compared to physical execution times:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Gradient-Boosted Ranker (LightGBM):} Optimized directly for ranking using LambdaRank (optimizing NDCG), transforming expert relevance into a per-query rank.
    \item \textbf{Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP):} A streamlined 2-layer network trained with pointwise MSE to predict individual expert relevance.
    \item \textbf{Graph Neural Network (GNN):} Utilizes learned expert embeddings and graph message passing to capture dependencies between different sub-benchmarks.
\end{itemize}

We explicitly contrast these learning-based routers against static heuristics. Strategies such as \texttt{greedy\_fastest} (always selecting tests with the shortest wall-clock time), \texttt{greedy\_slowest}, or fixed CPU/I/O mixes fail to adapt to unseen system states. By conditioning selection on real-time telemetry, the router avoids wasting time on globally fast but locally uninformative tests.

\paragraph{End-to-End Evaluation and the Accuracy-Cost Trade-off.}
Router models are not evaluated in isolation based solely on their training loss. Instead, \ourmethod utilizes a $3 \times 3$ grid evaluation (combining the 3 Router variants with 3 Reconstructor models) to assess end-to-end performance. The ultimate selection metric is the final reconstructed suite error (MAE and RMSE) produced by the combined pipeline.

This design frames benchmark acceleration as an explicit accuracy-cost trade-off, managed through two mechanisms:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Top-$K$ Sweep:} By evaluating configurations from $K=1$ through full set, the system balances the execution time saved against the reconstruction error. A combined balanced score penalizes configurations that yield high error or fail to deliver meaningful time savings.
    \item \textbf{Uncertainty-Guided Active Refinement:} A fixed Top-$K$ budget may be insufficient for highly anomalous systems. After executing the initial subset, the reconstruction model predicts the full-suite score $\hat{y}_{\mathrm{suite}}$ alongside its statistical uncertainty $\sigma_{\mathrm{suite}}$. If the uncertainty exceeds a predefined threshold ($\sigma_{\mathrm{suite}} \leq \tau_{\sigma}$), \ourmethod dynamically selects the unexecuted expert with the highest predicted variance:
    $$
    e_{\mathrm{next}}=\arg\max_{e_i \notin \mathcal{S}} \sigma_i
    $$
    This extra test is executed, merged into the observation vector, and the reconstruction is invoked again, repeating until confidence is achieved or the execution budget is exhausted.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Time-Bounded Probing}
\label{subsec:time-bounded-probing}

In addition to reducing the number of executed sub-benchmarks, \ourmethod further reduces the evaluation cost of each selected expert through time-bounded probing. Instead of running an iterative sub-benchmark until its official loop completes, \ourmethod executes a short probe for a predefined time window and leverages the collected telemetry to estimate the full sub-benchmark score. 

This mechanism differs fundamentally from confidence-based adaptive early stopping. The probe duration is strictly clamped within a fixed, safe operational window (e.g., $1$ to $30$ seconds) to avoid runaway executions caused by anomalous inputs. \ourmethod does not repeatedly query a model to decide whether to halt; rather, it enforces a hard wall-clock limit and uses a supervised estimator to map the truncated execution signature to the final benchmark score.

\paragraph{Dual-Mode Probing: Micro and Real.}
To accommodate diverse benchmark characteristics, \ourmethod supports two probing modes:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Micro-probe Mode:} The system executes a lightweight, category-aligned synthetic workload (e.g., CPU-intensive, syscall-intensive). This mode avoids invoking the heavy initialization logic of the original benchmark, providing a low-overhead approximation of the targeted subsystem.
    \item \textbf{Real-probe Mode:} \ourmethod invokes the original benchmark component but wraps it in a strict system-level timeout (e.g., \texttt{timeout <duration\_s + margin>}). If the subtest fails to complete within the budget, it is forcibly terminated.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Engineering Robustness over Outlier Rejection.}
Unlike conventional ML pipelines that aggressively discard truncated executions, timeouts, or noisy runs as statistical outliers, \ourmethod embraces these execution anomalies as measurable system states. In production environments, telemetry collection is often imperfect due to permission restrictions or heavy load. \ourmethod handles these gracefully:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Encoding Truncation as Features:} If a real probe is killed by the timeout, the event is not discarded. Instead, flags such as \texttt{real\_timed\_out}, \texttt{workload\_rc} (return code), and elapsed wall-clock time are explicitly encoded into the feature vector. The model learns to interpret the telemetry context of a forcefully truncated run.
    \item \textbf{Graceful Degradation for eBPF:} If high-fidelity eBPF tracing is unavailable (due to kernel restrictions or missing tools), the framework does not crash. It flags \texttt{ebpf\_available = 0} and zero-masks the relevant dimensions, allowing the estimator to infer based solely on standard \texttt{/proc} counters.
    \item \textbf{Rate Conversion:} To ensure telemetry is comparable regardless of the exact elapsed probe duration, monotonically increasing metrics (e.g., eBPF \texttt{sched\_switch} or \texttt{syscall\_enter}) are converted to per-second rates prior to vectorization.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Label Stabilization and Inference.}
The probe model is trained using historical full benchmark runs. During training construction, samples lacking valid ground-truth labels from full runs are safely filtered out. For benchmark suites with massive scoring variances across different hardware generations (e.g., Phoronix Test Suite), the primary prediction targets undergo $\log(1+x)$ (log1p) scaling to stabilize the loss gradients. Furthermore, to prevent overfitting on sparse data, the framework enforces a minimum sample threshold for per-test estimators. 

At inference time, \ourmethod simply executes the bounded probe, processes the robust feature vector, and predicts the scaled full-run score. This design changes the cost of evaluating selected subtests from an unpredictable, unbounded benchmark duration to a fixed and highly controllable probing budget.

\subsection{Reconstructor: Full-Suite Result Recovery}
\label{subsec:reconstructor}

After the router selects and executes a small subset of sub-benchmarks, \ourmethod relies on a reconstructor to recover the full benchmark outcome. The reconstructor addresses the sparse observation problem: given the current system feature vector and the partial subtest results, it acts as a multi-output regression model to simultaneously predict the scores of all unexecuted sub-benchmarks as well as the aggregate suite score.

\paragraph{Input Representation and Multi-Output Target.}
To make sparse benchmark results consumable by a fixed-size tensor, \ourmethod encodes all sub-benchmarks in a canonical order. Each sub-benchmark is represented by a 3-tuple: $z_i = (m_i, v_i, t_i)$, where $m_i \in \{0,1\}$ is a binary observation mask, $v_i$ is the observed score (if executed), and $t_i$ is the observed execution time. For unexecuted tests, the tuple is zero-filled. 
The final input vector concatenates the system context $x$ with the masked partial observations:
$$
X = [x,\, m_1, v_1, t_1,\, \ldots,\, m_n, v_n, t_n]
$$
The output target is the complete benchmark profile derived from historical full runs: $Y = [r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_n, S]$, where $S$ is the final reported index. For tree-based models (e.g., LightGBM, XGBoost), \ourmethod wraps the base regressor with a multi-output strategy to train an independent regressor per target dimension.

\paragraph{Training via Simulated Sparse Execution.}
Historical datasets exclusively contain complete benchmark runs. To teach the reconstructor how to recover full results from sparse router selections, \ourmethod employs a dynamic masking augmentation strategy during training. Each complete historical run is expanded into multiple simulated partial observations. For each augmentation pass, the framework uniformly samples a subset size $k \in [k_{\min}, k_{\max}]$, randomly selects $k$ subtests to act as the "executed" set, and masks the rest. This robust augmentation exposes the model to diverse sparsity patterns, preventing it from over-relying on any single subtest.

\paragraph{Scale Compression for Heterogeneous Targets.}
Comprehensive suites like the Phoronix Test Suite (PTS) aggregate highly heterogeneous workloads whose primary metrics span drastically different magnitudes (e.g., millions of operations per second vs. sub-millisecond latencies). To prevent workloads with massive numerical scales from dominating the loss gradients, \ourmethod applies domain-aware scale compression. Target variables spanning large orders of magnitude undergo $\log(1+x)$ transformations, and repeated profile outcomes are aggregated via log-mean. This stabilizes the training process without requiring complex, instance-weighted loss functions.

\paragraph{Uncertainty Estimation over Forced Rebalancing.}
A common challenge in system telemetry is the long-tail distribution of machine states; certain hardware configurations or severe contention scenarios appear rarely in the training data. Instead of forcefully rebalancing the dataset using synthetic oversampling or focal loss---which risks distorting the natural distribution of system states---\ourmethod embraces a system-level fail-safe: uncertainty estimation. 

Rather than blindly trusting predictions on rare machine states, \ourmethod trains the reconstructor to quantify its own confidence. For MLP implementations, \ourmethod utilizes a heteroscedastic network architecture trained via Gaussian Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) to output both the predicted mean and a log-variance for each subtest. For tree-based models, \ourmethod trains an auxiliary residual model on the primary model's absolute training errors (i.e., $|y - \hat{y}|$) to serve as a proxy for variance ($\sigma$). 

Consequently, if the reconstructor encounters an anomalous, out-of-distribution system state, it will output a high uncertainty variance. As described in Section~\ref{subsec:router}, this uncertainty directly triggers the active refinement loop, instructing the system to physically execute more subtests rather than relying on a low-confidence prediction.



\section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:evaluation}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{subsec:exp-setup}

We evaluate \ourmethod on five heterogeneous Linux hosts.
UnixBench and \textsc{PTS-CPU} are evaluated on all five machines; \textsc{PTS-GPU} is evaluated only on H1 (32U128G), the sole host equipped with an NVIDIA GPU---the remaining four hosts are CPU-only and do not run GPU workloads.
Our evaluation is organized around two complementary acceleration routes.
\textbf{Route~A} combines conditional expert selection with score reconstruction: a router chooses a Top-$K$ subset of sub-benchmarks, executes them, and a reconstructor predicts the full-suite score from partial observations.
\textbf{Route~B} applies time-bounded probing: each sub-benchmark is observed through a short execution window (with optional eBPF telemetry), and per-component scores are estimated and aggregated into a suite-level prediction.
Unless stated otherwise, each host trains and evaluates only on its own collected runs, so reported results reflect per-machine generalization rather than cross-host pooling.
All numeric results in the tables below are left as placeholders and will be filled after the full experimental campaign completes.

\subsubsection{Testbeds}
\label{subsubsec:testbeds}

We deploy \ourmethod on five Linux machines spanning a wide range of CPU and memory capacities.
Table~\ref{tab:testbeds} summarizes the hardware configuration of each host and the benchmark suites executed on it.
H1 (32 logical CPUs, 128\,GiB RAM, NVIDIA GPU) serves as the development server and is the only machine on which \textsc{PTS-GPU} is run; H2--H5 are smaller CPU-only instances used for UnixBench and \textsc{PTS-CPU} evaluation.
All machines share the same software stack (kernel, compiler toolchain, and benchmark versions) modulo platform-specific GPU drivers on H1.
We label hosts by a compact \texttt{CPU$\times$RAM} shorthand used throughout this section and in Section~2.

\paragraph{Software environment.}
Each host uses a Linux kernel with standard \texttt{perf} and optional \texttt{bpftrace} support where permitted.
System feature collection (\(\mathbf{x}\)) uses a fixed warmup window of 3\,s, \texttt{/proc} sampling interval of 0.5\,s, and a 64\,MiB in-process warmup working set unless noted otherwise.
When \texttt{perf} PMU counters are blocked (e.g., due to \texttt{kernel.perf\_event\_paranoid}), the collector degrades to \texttt{/proc}-based proxies without aborting the pipeline.
For GPU workloads on H1, NVIDIA driver and OpenCL inventory are collected when available; on CPU-only hosts (H2--H5), GPU dimensions are zero-masked at inference time.

\paragraph{Per-host training protocol.}
For every host \(h \in \{\mathrm{H1},\ldots,\mathrm{H5}\}\), we collect benchmark datasets locally and train all models using only runs whose session tags match \(h\).
H1 trains and evaluates on UnixBench, \textsc{PTS-CPU}, and \textsc{PTS-GPU}; H2--H5 train and evaluate on UnixBench and \textsc{PTS-CPU} only.
This isolates each machine's router, reconstructor, and probe models from other hosts' data distributions.
Cross-host comparison therefore reflects how \ourmethod behaves under different hardware ceilings rather than a single global model transferred across machines.

\subsubsection{Benchmark Suites}
\label{subsubsec:benchmark-suites}

We evaluate on three benchmark suites that stress complementary subsystems.
UnixBench and \textsc{PTS-CPU} are run on all five hosts; \textsc{PTS-GPU} is restricted to H1 because the other four machines lack discrete GPUs.

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{UnixBench (UB).} A classic system-level suite with 12 single-copy subtests (\(N=12\)), including CPU kernels (\texttt{dhry2reg}, \texttt{whetstone-double}), I/O (\texttt{fstime}, \texttt{fsbuffer}, \texttt{fsdisk}), and OS/interaction workloads (\texttt{pipe}, \texttt{context1}, \texttt{spawn}, \texttt{syscall}, \texttt{shell1}, \texttt{shell8}).
    We run UnixBench with a single parallel copy (\texttt{perl Run -c 1}), matching the \ourmethod{} collection protocol.
    The aggregate metric is the \emph{System Benchmarks Index Score}.
    Evaluated on all five hosts.

    \item \textbf{Phoronix Test Suite --- CPU (\textsc{PTS-CPU}).} The standard \texttt{cpu} suite with approximately 13 profiles covering compilation, cryptography, compression, and numerical kernels.
    Profile-level primary values span large dynamic ranges; suite aggregation follows log-mean over profiles, consistent with our reconstructor training target.
    Evaluated on all five hosts.

    \item \textbf{Phoronix Test Suite --- GPU (\textsc{PTS-GPU}).} The \texttt{pts/nvidia-gpu-compute} suite, executed only on H1 (32U128G), which has a suitable NVIDIA GPU and installed PTS profiles.
    This suite complements CPU-centric evaluation with OpenCL/GPU compute workloads and is omitted on H2--H5.
\end{itemize}

For Route~A end-to-end grid experiments on PTS, ground-truth full-suite scores are taken from previously collected full runs on the same host (offline replay), avoiding repeated full-suite online execution that can cause excessive wall time or resource exhaustion.
UnixBench grid experiments execute both partial and full runs online unless otherwise noted.

\subsubsection{Collected Data}
\label{subsubsec:collected-data}

\paragraph{Phase~1: Full-suite collection (shared by Routes~A and~B).}
On each host, we collect multiple complete benchmark sessions (typically 3--5 rounds per session) for every suite applicable to that host (UnixBench and \textsc{PTS-CPU} on all five hosts; \textsc{PTS-GPU} on H1 only).
Each run record stores:
(i)~system context \(\mathbf{x}\) (static + dynamic features),
(ii)~per-component results \(\mathbf{y}\) and timings \(\mathbf{t}\),
and (iii)~expert metadata (component identifiers, categories, and titles).
These runs provide supervision for router training, reconstructor training, probe label construction, and ground-truth evaluation.

\paragraph{Phase~2: Route~A model training and grid evaluation.}
For each applicable suite on each host, we train three router architectures (LightGBM ranker, MLP, GNN-expert) and three reconstructors (XGBoost, LightGBM, MLP), then evaluate all \(3 \times 3 = 9\) end-to-end combinations.
Each combination produces one experiment report with predicted suite score, actual full-suite score, partial execution time, and full execution time (or dataset-replay ground truth for PTS).

\paragraph{Phase~3: Route~B probe pipeline.}
For each applicable suite on each host, we build a probe dataset by executing short probes (default 4\,s per component, micro-probe mode) over historical full runs on the same host, train two regressors (LightGBM and XGBoost; PTS uses log1p labels with per-profile estimators), and run an online experiment that re-probes all components and compares the predicted suite score against the most recent full run on that host.

\paragraph{Phase~4: Supplementary offline studies (Route~A, best combination).}
After selecting the best router--reconstructor pair per suite from Phase~2 on each applicable host, we conduct three supplementary studies on stored runs only (leave-one-session-out cross-validation, no re-execution):
Top-$K$ sweep, routing-policy comparison, and system-feature ablation.
For \textsc{PTS-GPU}, supplementary studies use H1 data only.

\subsubsection{Metrics}
\label{subsubsec:metrics}

\paragraph{Accuracy.}
For suite-level score \(\hat{S}\) and ground truth \(S\), we report:
\emph{absolute error} \(| \hat{S} - S |\),
\emph{relative error} \(| \hat{S} - S | / \max(|S|, \epsilon)\),
and rank-correlation metrics (Spearman/Kendall) where cross-run ranking is meaningful.
For offline cross-validation studies, we also report out-of-fold MAE and RMSE on the suite dimension.

\paragraph{Cost.}
We measure \emph{wall-clock time} of benchmark execution:
\(T_{\mathrm{partial}}\) for the executed subset,
\(T_{\mathrm{full}}\) for the complete suite (or dataset-replay equivalent),
and \emph{fraction saved} \((T_{\mathrm{full}} - T_{\mathrm{partial}}) / T_{\mathrm{full}}\).
Route~B additionally reports total probe wall time and per-component probe duration.

\paragraph{Combined trade-off score.}
For Top-$K$ and routing-policy studies, we rank configurations using a \emph{balanced score} that penalizes high suite MAE and low time savings (lower is better), enabling Pareto-style comparison between accuracy and cost.

\paragraph{Aggregation across hosts.}
For UnixBench and \textsc{PTS-CPU}, we summarize each metric by mean (and optionally standard deviation) over the five testbeds unless a table explicitly reports per-host columns.
For \textsc{PTS-GPU}, all reported values come from H1 (32U128G) only.
Statistical significance testing will be reported where applicable after all runs complete.

\label{subsec:overall-effectiveness}

We first ask whether \ourmethod can approximate full-suite scores with substantially lower execution cost than running every component to completion.
For each applicable host--suite pair, we compare:
\textbf{(i)} full-suite execution (baseline),
\textbf{(ii)} Route~A with the best \(3 \times 3\) combination selected from the grid on that host,
and \textbf{(iii)} Route~B with the better of LightGBM vs.\ XGBoost probe models on that host.

UnixBench and \textsc{PTS-CPU} rows aggregate over five hosts; \textsc{PTS-GPU} rows report H1 (32U128G) only.
We expect Route~A to dominate when partial sub-benchmark execution remains informative for reconstruction, while Route~B should achieve the lowest execution footprint when short probes suffice.

\subsection{Routing Strategy Comparison}
\label{subsec:routing-strategy}

Subset selection strategy strongly influences both cost and reconstruction quality.
At fixed \(K = K^\star\) from Section~\ref{subsec:topk-tradeoff}, we compare seven policies:
\texttt{random} (seeded uniform subset),
\texttt{fixed\_first\_k} (canonical order prefix),
\texttt{fixed\_cpu\_mix} and \texttt{fixed\_io\_mix} (heuristic CPU/IO presets; on PTS, degenerates to canonical prefix when IDs do not match),
\texttt{greedy\_slowest} and \texttt{greedy\_fastest} (by historical wall time on the held-out sample),
and \texttt{router} (Top-$K$ from the trained router).
All policies share the same reconstructor and cross-validation protocol.
UnixBench and \textsc{PTS-CPU} results are aggregated over five hosts; \textsc{PTS-GPU} results are from H1 only.

Table~\ref{tab:routing-policy} summarizes suite MAE, time saved, and balanced score.
We hypothesize that \texttt{router} achieves the best trade-off by conditioning on \(\mathbf{x}\), while static heuristics fail on heterogeneous hosts (e.g., I/O-bound vs.\ CPU-bound configurations).

\subsection{Summary of Findings}
\label{subsec:eval-summary}

Our evaluation on five heterogeneous Linux hosts is designed to answer four questions.
We run UnixBench and \textsc{PTS-CPU} on all five machines and \textsc{PTS-GPU} on H1 only.
\textbf{Q1:} Can Route~A approximate full-suite scores with significantly less execution time than the baseline?
\textbf{Q2:} Which router--reconstructor combination generalizes best per suite?
\textbf{Q3:} How should practitioners choose \(K\), subset policy, and telemetry groups under an accuracy--cost budget?
\textbf{Q4:} Can Route~B further reduce execution footprint via fixed-duration probing, and which probe regressor is preferable?

After all experiments complete, we will summarize findings as follows (placeholders to be replaced with measured conclusions):

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Overall effectiveness (Q1).} Route~A reduces UnixBench wall time by \textbf{[TBD]\%} on average with \textbf{[TBD]\%} mean relative suite error; Route~B achieves \textbf{[TBD]\%} error at \textbf{[TBD]\,s} total probe time vs.\ \textbf{[TBD]\,s} full-suite time (Table~\ref{tab:overall-effectiveness}).

    \item \textbf{Model combinations (Q2).} The best Route~A pair per suite is \textbf{[TBD router]} + \textbf{[TBD reconstructor]} for UnixBench (five hosts), \textbf{[TBD]} for \textsc{PTS-CPU} (five hosts), and \textbf{[TBD]} for \textsc{PTS-GPU} (H1 only) (Tables~\ref{tab:model-combination-ub}--\ref{tab:model-combination-pts-gpu}).

    \item \textbf{Accuracy--cost trade-off (Q3a).} Recommended subset sizes are \(K^\star_{\mathrm{UB}}=\textbf{[TBD]}\), \(K^\star_{\mathrm{CPU}}=\textbf{[TBD]}\), and \(K^\star_{\mathrm{GPU}}=\textbf{[TBD]}\) on H1 (Table~\ref{tab:topk-sweep}).

    \item \textbf{Routing policies (Q3b).} The learned \texttt{router} policy outperforms static heuristics by \textbf{[TBD]} balanced-score margin on average for UnixBench and \textsc{PTS-CPU} across five hosts, and on H1 for \textsc{PTS-GPU} (Table~\ref{tab:routing-policy}).

    \item \textbf{Feature importance (Q3c).} Dynamic PMU/proc features contribute \textbf{[TBD]} \(\Delta\)MAE when removed; GPU/OpenCL features matter most for \textsc{PTS-GPU} on H1 (Table~\ref{tab:feature-ablation}).

    \item \textbf{Probe route (Q4).} \textbf{[LightGBM / XGBoost]} yields lower suite error on \textbf{[TBD]} of 11 host--suite pairs (five UnixBench + five \textsc{PTS-CPU} + one \textsc{PTS-GPU}); probe-based evaluation uses \textbf{[TBD]\%} of full-suite wall time (Table~\ref{tab:probe-models}).
\end{itemize}

These results collectively demonstrate that \ourmethod makes full-suite benchmarking practical in settings where repeated, low-disruption measurement is required---including multi-machine comparison, configuration tuning, and production-adjacent monitoring---without abandoning the interpretability of established suite scores.
